The Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 was moved to require active consent from class action members, cap funder and lawyer shares at 30% of proceeds, and mandate court approval of distributions to ensure fair returns for claimants, citing cases like Banksia Securities and Wittenbury v Vocation where funders and lawyers took nearly 50% of settlements.

The speaker argued the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 is Orwellian and will harm ordinary Australians' access to justice, citing a 30 per cent cap on costs and a switch to opt-in class actions as design features that benefit defendants. He announced Labor will oppose the bill and move a second reading amendment, referencing the robodebt scheme (430,000 victims, $1.7 billion restitution) and an underpaid Aboriginal wages case as examples of class actions that would be prevented.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 is needed to regulate litigation funders and ensure class action members receive at least 70% of claim proceeds, with a rebuttable presumption against non-member distributions exceeding 30%. The bill responds to Australian Law Reform Commission findings showing median plaintiff returns drop from 85% (without funders) to 51% (with funders), and to a parliamentary committee’s 31 recommendations.

The Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 would restrict access to class actions for many Australians, particularly victims of financial fraud like those from the Trio Capital collapse, by imposing court approval requirements and a rebuttable presumption that distributions under 70% to plaintiffs are unfair. The bill was criticised for its rushed inquiry process, which gave the public only days to respond, and for potentially discouraging settlements, increasing costs, and benefiting wealthy defendants over ordinary plaintiffs.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 addresses the free rider problem in open class actions by establishing a new managed investment scheme for litigation funding and requiring fair and reasonable returns to funders, based on recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services and the Australian Law Reform Commission.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment Bill, arguing that class actions are the only means of redress for people harmed by government and corporate actions—citing Queensland taxi owners, stolen wages for Indigenous Australians, and the live cattle export ban—and warned of personal retaliation against those who destroy livelihoods.

The speech supported the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing that litigation funders exploit vulnerable plaintiffs by taking large shares of court-awarded compensation. It argued for stronger regulation and court oversight of litigation funding contracts while affirming that class actions remain legal.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 is a deceptive attempt by the Morrison-Joyce government to protect wealthy defendants by making class actions harder for everyday Australians, contrary to its stated consumer protection purpose. They cited opposition from the Law Council, Phi Finney McDonald, and defendant lawyers at Herbert Smith Freehills, and noted constitutional concerns raised by Justice Beach and former Solicitor-General Justin Gleeson SC, as well as specific class actions—including stolen wages, stolen generations, Westpac overcharging, PFAS contamination, and Domino’s underpayment cases—that would not have proceeded under the bill.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment Bill 2021 would harm access to justice by making class actions harder, citing that community legal centres turn away over 160,000 people annually and that the bill would have required 430,000 robodebt class action members to opt in. The speaker announced Labor's opposition to the bill.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would restrict class actions by requiring court approval for funding agreements over 30% and shifting from an opt-out to an opt-in system, thereby making it harder for ordinary Australians, particularly remote and Indigenous communities, to access justice.

The speaker argued the bill is misleadingly titled and will actually hinder access to justice by protecting wealthy defendants, citing constitutional concerns, a rushed and inadequate consultation process, and examples of landmark class actions—such as stolen wages and environmental contamination cases—that would be blocked under its measures.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would harm access to justice by making class actions harder to bring. They cited examples such as a $500 million settlement for 2009 Victorian bushfire survivors, a $112 million robodebt class action for 450,000 people, and actions against major banks and Sigma Pharmaceuticals, and noted concerns from legal expert Justin Gleeson that the bill may be unconstitutional.

The speaker opposed the 30% cap on litigation funder fees in the Corporations Amendment Bill, arguing it would reduce access to justice for small businesses and individuals by altering funders' risk-reward calculations. He cited high legal costs, a defamation case costing nearly $2 million without trial, and discrepancies between TGA and AusVaxSafety data on COVID vaccine adverse events.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would replace the opt-out class action model with an opt-in requirement and flawed fund distribution rules, making class actions harder for ordinary Australians while protecting large corporations. They urged the government to withdraw or vote against the bill.

The speaker supported the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would ensure class action claimants receive a fairer share of damages by capping litigation funders’ take at 30% and citing cases where claimants received as little as 33% of settlements.

The speaker argued the bill makes justice harder for ordinary Australians, citing expert John Sheahan's view that it "makes things worse for everyone." They opposed the 70-30 cost split and opt-in requirement, claiming these will block meritorious claims and protect large corporate defendants, while criticizing the rushed three-week committee process and lack of a proper regulatory impact statement.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 would fundamentally weaken class actions by shifting from an opt-out to an opt-in structure, denying access to justice for vulnerable people, especially in rural, regional and remote communities. They also criticised the bill's process as atrocious and biased, and claimed it was possibly unconstitutional and driven by ideology rather than evidence.

The bill introduces a new annual charge on all higher education providers registered with TEQSA to recover the costs of its risk monitoring and regulatory oversight activities, with the amount to be set by regulations. The charge will be phased in from 1 January 2022 (20% of costs in 2022, 50% in 2023, 100% in 2024) and is expected to collect around $5.7 million annually, replacing the current partial recovery of about 15% of TEQSA's total costs.

The bills increase TEQSA's cost recovery from about 15% to full cost through higher application fees (from 1 January 2022) and a new annual charge phased in at 20% in 2022, 50% in 2023 and 100% in 2024, originally announced in the 2018–19 budget but delayed due to COVID-19.

The speaker supported the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Charges) Bill 2021 and the amendment bill, arguing that higher education providers should pay increased cost recovery fees—phased in over three years—to fund TEQSA’s regulatory activities, noting that current cost recovery is about 15% and that the sector had $38 billion in revenue in 2017.

Labor opposes the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Charges) Bill 2021, arguing that the cost‑recovery measure unfairly burdens a higher education sector already devastated by 17,000 job losses, a 10% real funding cut over three years, soaring student debt of $60,000, and a government‑driven brain drain of researchers.

The speaker supported the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Charges) Bill 2021 and related amendment, which phase in increased cost recovery for TEQSA from 15% to full cost by 2024, and noted $245 million in federal funding for Edith Cowan University's new Perth campus, set to open in 2025 with $695 million total cost.

The speaker argued for passing the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency cost recovery bills, with fee waivers during COVID and a three-year transition from 2022; they cited $1.5 billion in additional support for public universities, $53 million for private providers, and rebutted opposition claims by stating no public university met JobSeeker eligibility thresholds (30% revenue decline) and that several universities—including Monash ($267M surplus), Melbourne ($178M), Flinders ($35M), USQ ($12M), and Western Sydney ($13M)—reported surpluses in 2020.

This bill updates the law to introduce a new charge on registered higher education providers, replacing some fees with a broader cost recovery model.
The charge would be set by regulations, with the agency consulting stakeholders on a draft implementation statement before the rules are made.
The charge starts at 20% of costs on 1 January 2022, rises to 50% in 2023, and reaches full cost recovery by 1 January 2024.
The bill requires higher education providers to pay the new charge and any late payment penalties.
Non-payment of the charge would breach a registration condition and could lead to enforcement by the agency.
The bill allows the agency to issue guidelines to help administer the charge.

The speaker corrected an error in the second reading speech for the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (2021 Measures No. 1) Bill 2021, clarifying that the bill does not remove captioning requirements for regional and remote broadcasters beyond those for metropolitan broadcasters.

The bill halves Foxtel's Australian drama expenditure obligation from 10% to 5% and extends the Regional and Small Publishers Innovation Fund deadline. Labor will move to delete the schedule reducing Foxtel's obligation, arguing the government is dismantling Australian content rules for broadcasters without imposing corresponding requirements on streaming services like Netflix.

The bill updates broadcasting regulations to create a level playing field between traditional broadcasters and new streaming services like Netflix and Stan. It extends the Regional and Small Publishers Innovation Fund deadline past June 2021 to ensure regional publishers, including those in the Mid North Coast, can access grants of up to $400,000.

The speaker opposed the halving of Foxtel's Australian screen content expenditure obligation from 10% to 5% in the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (2021 Measures No. 1) Bill 2021, arguing it would undermine local content quotas and harm the creative industry. They supported an amendment by the member for Greenway to excise that section from the bill.

The bill addresses regulatory anomalies from digital disruption and population growth, including captioning services, digital radio spectrum, and overlapping radio licensees facing fines of up to $444,000, while also calling for video-on-demand platforms to meet the same content quotas as traditional broadcasters.

The speaker supported the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (2021 Measures No. 1) Bill 2021, arguing that mandated local content requirements are outdated and mainly benefit Sydney and Melbourne. He advocated for a shift toward encouraging high-quality Australian content for global streaming platforms, citing the SA Film Corporation's $50 million production *Mortal Kombat* as an example.

The member for Indi supported schedule 5 of the bill to extend the Regional and Small Publishers Innovation Fund beyond June 2021, and called on the government to also replenish the fund, noting grant recipients in her electorate including Alexandra Newspapers and the Corryong Courier. She also expressed disappointment over the impending end of the Nine News Border North East nightly bulletin on 30 June.

The speech opposed the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (2021 Measures No. 1) Bill, arguing it would halve subscription TV drama investment from $25 million to $12.5 million, impose no obligations on streaming services, and continue cuts to the ABC, which has lost $780 million since 2013 and 250 jobs last year. It also cited PwC projections that eliminating quotas would cut Australian drama by 90% and end children's programs.

The speaker opposed halving Foxtel's Australian screen content obligations from 10% to 5% while supporting other minor regulatory changes, and criticised the government for lacking a long-term vision for Australian broadcasting and publishing.

The member for Macnamara argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (2021 Measures No. 1) Bill 2021 undermines Australian creative industries by reducing Australian content quotas for Foxtel, and criticised the exclusion of creative workers from JobKeeper. He also called on the City of Port Phillip to reverse its decision to end funding for six local arts organisations—Australian Tapestry Workshop, Phillip Adams BalletLab, Rawcus Theatre Company, Red Stitch Actors Theatre, Theatre Works, and the Torch—and condemned ongoing cuts to the ABC.

The government argued the bill reduces regulatory burdens on Australia's media industry, including recalibrating drama expenditure obligations for subscription broadcasters, simplifying subscription TV captioning rules, clarifying grandfathering powers for regional radio broadcasters, removing redundant digital radio planning requirements, and extending the time frame for the Regional and Small Publishers Innovation Fund grants into 2021-22.

The speaker argued that the minister is incompetent after he gave an incorrect second reading speech on the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (2021 Measures No. 1) Bill 2021 and was repudiated by the Senate crossbench and his own government. They criticised the minister for halving Foxtel’s Australian content obligations, failing to impose a 5% streaming content quota, suspending commercial TV quotas improperly, and kicking community TV off the air, while also losing the confidence of his own side.

The bill was introduced in order to amend the [Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environment_Protection_and_Biodiversity_Conservation_Act_1999) (EPBC Act) in order to establish: * *a framework for making, varying, revoking and applying National Environmental Standards and* * *an Environment Assurance Commissioner (EAC) to monitor and audit the operation of bilateral agreements with the states and territories as well as to oversee Commonwealth processes under the EPBC Act for making and enforcing approval decisions.* The [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2021a/21bd074) sets out the following 'Key Issues' relating to the bill: * *Industry groups broadly support the Bill, including the framework for National Environmental Standards and the proposed EAC. They consider this Bill, together with the Streamlining Bill, would provide certainty and clarity while addressing regulatory duplication in environmental approvals. However, several industry groups suggest that any National Environmental Standards made under the Bill should reflect the existing requirements of the EPBC Act.* * *Other stakeholders, including environmental, legal and scientific organisations, generally do not support the Bill, expressing considerable concern. Many noted the lack of a comprehensive government response to the Final Report of the Samuel Review, and suggested that the Government was ‘cherry picking’ recommendations and making piecemeal reforms, rather than implementing the full range of ‘tranche 1’ reforms identified in the Final Repor

The majority voted in favour of *disagreeing* with [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2021-06-23.148.1) introduced by Warringah MP [Zali Steggall](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/warringah/zali_steggall) (Independent), which means they failed. According to MP Steggall, these amendments would "*ensure that measures to safeguard the environment are in place in relation to the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021.*" She explained the purpose of each one in detail in her [contribution to the debate](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2021-06-23.148.2). ### Amendment text > *(1) Schedule 1, item 6, page 5 (line 6), omit "may", substitute "must".* > > *(2) Schedule 1, item 6, page 5 (line 13), omit "may", substitute "must".* > > *(3) Schedule 1, item 6, page 5 (after line 16), after subsection 65C(1), insert:* > >> *(1A) Without limiting subsection (1), the standards made under that subsection must include national standards for each of the following:* >> >>> *(a) matters of national environmental significance;* >>> >>> *(b) transparent processes and robust decisions, including:* >>> >>>> *(i) judicial review; and* >>>> >>>> *(ii) community consultation; and* >>>> >>>> *(iii) adequate assessment of impacts on matters of national environmental significance, including climate impacts; and* >>>> >>> *(iv) emissions profile disclosure; and* >>>> >>>> *(v) regional planning;* >>> >>> *(c) Indigenous engagement and involvement in environmental decision making;* >>> >>> *(d) compliance and enforcement;* >>> >>> *(e) data and information;* >>> >>> *(f) environmental monitoring and evaluation of outcomes;* >>> >>> *(g) environmental restoration, including offsets;* >>> >>> *(h) wildlife permits and trade.* >> >> *(1B) The Minister must take all reasonable steps to ensure that national environmental standards are in force, and comply with subsection (1A), at all times.

The speaker argued that the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 should be passed to modernise environmental laws through competitive federalism, balancing conservation with economic development, and criticised binary framings of environment versus commerce. He called on the Labor Party to support the bill, referencing Graeme Samuel's review and the need to advance Western Australian projects.

The speaker argued that the government's EPBC Amendment Bill is a rehash of failed 2014 Abbott-era legislation, ignores the Samuel review's recommendations, and fails to provide stronger environmental protections or address delays in project approvals. He moved an amendment noting the government's failure to deliver durable reform and called for a genuine first-stage reform package with stronger standards, independent oversight, and adequate resourcing.

The speaker argued that the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 should provide greater certainty and consistency in project approvals, citing the New Acland mine’s 14-year delay affecting 350 workers, and noted that all state and territory leaders have agreed to streamline approvals and develop national environmental standards.

Labor opposed the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021, arguing it weakens environmental laws during a biodiversity crisis. The speech cited Auditor-General findings that timely approval decisions dropped from 60% (2014–15) to 5% (2018–19) and 79% of approvals were non‑compliant, and called for stronger protections, a genuinely independent assurance commissioner, and adoption of Professor Graeme Samuel’s review recommendations.

The speaker argued that the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 would weaken environmental protections by replacing the stronger interim national standards recommended by Professor Graeme Samuel’s independent review with inferior government-drafted standards, allowing the minister to make decisions inconsistent with those standards if deemed in the public interest, and creating an environmental assurance commissioner with no power to investigate individual project decisions—all while Australia already has the world’s highest rate of mammal extinctions and faces escalating climate change impacts.

The EPBC Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021 is inconsistent with the Samuel review and resurrects Tony Abbott's failed one-stop-shop approach. Citing ANAO data showing 95% of decisions are late and 79% noncompliant after 40% funding cuts, the bill was opposed in favour of the full Samuel package, including strong national standards, an independent regulator, and retained Commonwealth intervention powers.

The speaker argued that the bill cements the government's poor environmental record, citing 22 policies in eight years, a divided government, and a lack of firm targets—calling the net-zero 2050 commitment a mere "preference." They highlighted UNESCO's recommendation to list the Great Barrier Reef as endangered, criticised the government's response to Professor Graeme Samuel's review as falling short, and insisted on establishing an independent compliance watchdog with genuine enforcement powers.

The speaker argued the government's bill weakens environmental protections by rejecting expert recommendations, replacing "best available information" with "adequate information," and shifting federal responsibility to states. They opposed the bill, citing the government's poor environmental record, including a 510% increase in job and investment delays and 79% of approvals containing errors.

The bill was opposed as insufficient and contrary to Graeme Samuel's review findings, with the public interest exemption (subclause 65H(7)) allowing circumvention of national standards and the absence of an independent Environment Assurance Commissioner cited as major flaws. Amendments will be moved during consideration in detail to strengthen the standards and require independent expert review.

The speaker supported the EPBC Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021, arguing it implements the Samuel review's 38 recommendations to cut regulatory duplication and project delays, citing costs up to $47 million per month for greenfields projects. They listed specific treaties (World Heritage, Ramsar, IUCN, Bond conventions) and examples of state failures (Great Barrier Reef mining, Franklin dam, Kakadu, Coronation Hill, Murray-Darling Basin Plan), and noted that approval delays stem from public service cuts, not state control—pointing to fast approvals under the last Labor government for projects like Wheatstone, Queensland gas, Prelude, and Olympic Dam.

The government defended the EPBC Amendment (Standards and Assurance) Bill 2021, arguing it establishes national environmental standards and an environmental assurance commissioner as part of a staged reform process following the Samuel review. Treasury Laws Amendment (Self Managed Superannuation Funds) Act 2021
Biosecurity Amendment (Traveller Declarations and Other Measures) Bill 2020

The opposition moved an amendment to the Biosecurity Amendment Bill, supporting the bill but condemning the government for implementing only four of the ten Commonwealth-responsibility recommendations from the 2017 Craik biosecurity review, including the proposed container levy. It also criticised the government for lacking a strategic plan to achieve its $100 billion agriculture industry target.
Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Streamlining Environmental Approvals) Bill 2020

The opposition rejected the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Streamlining Environmental Approvals) Bill 2020 as premature, arguing the Samuel review found the EPBC Act serves neither the environment nor industry, and that the government failed to make a coherent case for the bill. The speaker also noted a $34 million stewardship package announced in March 2019 has not yet commenced, with programs not starting until 2021.
Primary Industries (Customs) Charges Amendment (Dairy Cattle Export Charge) Bill 2020

The opposition supported the Primary Industries (Customs) Charges Amendment (Dairy Cattle Export Charge) Bill 2020, but moved an amendment condemning the government for failing to develop a comprehensive plan to achieve the National Farmers’ Federation’s vision of a $100 billion agriculture industry by 2030, despite the Prime Minister’s promise at the Dubbo Bush Summit over a year ago. The speaker also noted that voluntary levy contributions had dropped from 92% in 2011 to 3% by 2019, and criticised the government for lacking an overarching strategic plan for agriculture, citing the Future Drought Fund as another example of headline numbers without follow-through.
Export Control Legislation Amendment (Certification of Narcotic Exports) Bill 2020

Supported the Export Control Legislation Amendment bill facilitating hemp seed exports to the United States, but moved an amendment condemning the government for lacking a strategic plan for agriculture, fisheries and forestry, criticized the ineffective 2015 agriculture white paper, and called for removal of the forestry water rule and reform of the 30-year-old agricultural research and development system.
Farm Household Support Amendment (Relief Measures) Bill (No. 1) 2020

The Labor member moved an amendment criticising the government's failed record on drought assistance, challenged the claimed $8 billion in drought spending as misleading, and argued for a national drought plan and bipartisan support for zero net emissions by 2050 to benefit farmers.

The Export Control Bill 2019 was welcomed as important but criticised for taking five years to introduce; a second reading amendment was moved condemning the government for lacking a comprehensive agricultural export plan, including a target of $100 billion in farm-gate value by 2030.
Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Amendment (Cross-boundary Greenhouse Gas Titles and Other Measures) Bill 2019

The opposition supported the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Amendment Bill 2019 but moved an amendment lamenting the government's failure to adequately promote carbon-reducing technologies, noting cuts to carbon capture and storage funding and a lack of economy-wide action on emissions reduction, electric vehicles, forestry abatement and hydrogen.
